quiz.q: A tea stall sold 236 cups of tea in the morning and 186 in the evening. How many cups in all?
quiz.explain: Ones 6 + 6 = 12, carry 1. Tens 3 + 8 + 1 = 12, carry 1. Hundreds 2 + 1 + 1 = 4. So 422.

teach.ask: Gappu added 47 + 28 and wrote 615! What went wrong? Explain carrying to him.
teach.praise: 15 ones is 1 ten and 5 ones! So 47 + 28 = 75. I get it now!
teach.nudge: What should I do when the ones add up to more than 9?

revise.summary: If a place adds up to 10 or more, make a ten or a hundred and carry it to the next place. Always add the carried number.
focus: Add 3-digit numbers with carrying.
Carry from ones to tens and from tens to hundreds.
Carry when a place makes exactly 10.
traps: Don't forget to add the carried 1.
Don't write both digits of 15 in the ones place.
Carry even when a place adds to exactly 10.

learn.hook: How do you take 7 away from 2? Borrow from the tens house next door!
points: Line up the places and subtract the ones first.
If the top ones digit is smaller, break 1 ten into 10 ones. This is called borrowing or regrouping.
352 − 127: 2 − 7 is not possible, so break a ten: 12 − 7 = 5. Tens: 4 − 2 = 2. Hundreds: 3 − 1 = 2. Answer 225.
If the top tens digit is too small, break 1 hundred into 10 tens.
Check by adding: 225 + 127 = 352.

example.q: A shop had 430 kites and sold 185. How many kites are left?
steps: Ones: 0 − 5 is not possible. Break a ten: 10 − 5 = 5. Now 2 tens are left.
Tens: 2 − 8 is not possible. Break a hundred: 12 − 8 = 4. Now 3 hundreds are left.

learn.reallife: Finding how many pages are left to read or how much money is left after shopping uses subtraction.

quiz.q: What is 463 − 128?
quiz.explain: 3 − 8 is not possible, so break a ten: 13 − 8 = 5. Tens: 5 − 2 = 3. Hundreds: 4 − 1 = 3. So 335.
quiz.mistake: Takes the smaller digit from the bigger one (8 − 3) instead of borrowing

quiz.q: A train had 275 passengers. 132 got off at Jaipur. How many passengers are on the train now?
quiz.explain: Ones 5 − 2 = 3, tens 7 − 3 = 4, hundreds 2 − 1 = 1. So 143.

quiz.q: A school has 520 children. 248 of them are girls. How many are boys?
quiz.explain: Ones: break a ten, 10 − 8 = 2. Tens: break a hundred, 11 − 4 = 7. Hundreds: 4 − 2 = 2. So 272.
quiz.mistake: Takes the smaller digit from the bigger one in each place instead of borrowing

quiz.q: What is 400 − 1?
quiz.explain: 1 less than 400 is 399. Counting back: 401, 400, 399.
quiz.mistake: Takes away from the hundreds instead of the ones

quiz.q: Kabir had ₹350. He spent ₹175. How much money is left?
quiz.mistake: Takes the smaller digit from the bigger one instead of borrowing

quiz.q: To check that 610 − 245 = 365, which addition should you do?
quiz.explain: Add the answer to the number taken away. 365 + 245 = 610, so the answer is right.
steps: To check a subtraction, add the answer to the number taken away.
quiz.mistake: Adds the two numbers from the question

quiz.q: In 342 − 118, the ones are 2 − 8. What should we do first?
quiz.explain: 2 is smaller than 8, so we break 1 ten from the tens place. Now we have 12 ones, and 12 − 8 = 4.
steps: Answer: Break 1 ten into 10 ones, making 12 − 8

quiz.q: Meena's storybook has 300 pages. She has read 126 pages. How many pages are left?
quiz.explain: 300 − 126: break a hundred into tens and a ten into ones. Ones 10 − 6 = 4, tens 9 − 2 = 7, hundreds 2 − 1 = 1. So 174.
quiz.mistake: Takes the smaller digit from the bigger one in each place

teach.ask: Gappu is doing 52 − 27. He says '2 − 7? I'll just do 7 − 2!' Help him do it the right way.
teach.praise: Break a ten, then 12 − 7 = 5. 52 − 27 = 25! I won't flip the digits again.
teach.nudge: If the top digit is smaller, where can I get more ones from?

revise.summary: To subtract, start with the ones. If the top digit is smaller, break 1 ten into 10 ones (or 1 hundred into 10 tens). Check by adding.
focus: Subtract 3-digit numbers with borrowing.
Break a ten or a hundred when needed.
Check by adding the answer and the number taken away.
traps: Don't take the smaller digit from the bigger one. Borrow.
Don't do 8 − 2 when the sum is 2 − 8.
To check, add the answer to the number taken away.

topics.title: Measuring with hand spans and steps

learn.hook: How long is your desk? Use your hand span and find out!
points: Length tells how long, how tall or how far something is.
We can measure with body parts: hand spans for a desk, footsteps for a room, arm lengths for a cloth.
A hand span is the stretch from the tip of the thumb to the tip of the little finger.
Different people get different answers, because hand spans are not the same size. A child's span is smaller than a teacher's.
To compare lengths, place things side by side: the longest ponytail, a string as long as the window.

example.q: Teacher measures the table as 6 spans. Riya measures it as 9 spans. Who has the bigger hand span?
steps: The same table needs fewer of a bigger unit.

learn.reallife: Tailors used to measure cloth by arm lengths. Now they use a measuring tape so everyone gets the same answer.

games.title: Measuring facts
items: A bigger hand span gives a smaller count.
Everyone's hand span is the same.
Length tells how long or tall something is.
Footsteps are good for measuring a pencil.
A pencil is too short for footsteps.

quiz.q: What does length tell us?
options: How long, tall or far something is
quiz.explain: Length is about how long, tall or far.
steps: Length is a kind of measure.
It tells how long, how tall or how far something is.
How heavy is weight. How much water is capacity.
Answer: How long, tall or far something is

quiz.q: Which is best to measure the length of a classroom?
quiz.explain: A room is long, so footsteps are quicker.
steps: For long things, a big unit is quicker.
Footsteps are bigger than spans or finger widths.

quiz.q: Ravi measures a bench as 8 spans. His father measures it as 5 spans. Why are they different?
options: Their hand spans are different sizes
quiz.explain: Father's span is bigger, so fewer spans fit.
steps: The bench is the same. Only the unit changed.
Father's span is bigger, so fewer spans fit: 5 instead of 8.
Answer: Their hand spans are different sizes

quiz.q: A desk is 4 spans long. Two desks side by side are how many spans?
quiz.explain: 4 + 4 = 8 spans.

quiz.q: Meena's ribbon is 7 spans and Gita's is 5 spans (same person measuring). Whose is longer?
quiz.explain: 7 spans is more than 5 spans.
steps: The same person measured both, so the unit is the same.

quiz.q: How can you find the longest ponytail in your class without a ruler?
options: Stand the girls side by side and compare
quiz.explain: Comparing side by side shows which is longest.
steps: To compare lengths, put things side by side.
Stand the girls side by side and compare ponytails.
Height is not the same as ponytail length.
Answer: Stand the girls side by side and compare
quiz.mistake: Mixes up height with ponytail length

quiz.q: Raju's room is 12 footsteps long. Mira's room is 9 footsteps (same person). How many more footsteps is Raju's room?
Why do people get different hand-span counts for the same table?
options: Their hands are of different sizes
quiz.explain: This is why we need a common unit everyone agrees on.
steps: People's hands are of different sizes.
So we need a common unit everyone agrees on.
Answer: Their hands are of different sizes

teach.ask: Gappu and his mother measured a twig with their wings and got different answers. Why?
teach.praise: Our wings are different sizes, so we need a common unit! Chirp!
teach.nudge: Are our wings the same size?

revise.summary: Length tells how long, how tall or how far something is. We can measure with hand spans, footsteps and arm lengths, but different people get different answers.
focus: Choose a good body unit for an object.
Compare lengths by placing things side by side.
Explain why counts differ between people.
remember: A hand span: tip of the thumb to tip of the little finger.
A bigger unit fits fewer times: teacher 6 spans, Riya 9 spans.
We need a common unit everyone agrees on.
traps: Length is not weight.
The object does not change when the count changes. The unit changed.
Don't use a tiny unit for a long thing.

learn.hook: How far is it from one classroom wall to the other? Steps, a rope, or a stick?
points: To find the distance between two walls, walk heel to toe, or lay a rope or stick again and again, and count.
A good method has no gaps and no overlaps, and uses the same unit every time.
To find the longest and shortest paper strings, place them side by side with one end matching.
To decorate a board, count how many strings fit around its border: top + bottom + 2 sides.

example.q: A board's border is 4 strings on top, 4 on the bottom and 2 on each side. How many strings in all?

learn.reallife: Painters and carpenters measure walls with long tapes before buying paint or wood.

games.title: Lengths
items: Thread to sew on a button
Kite string on a full reel

games.title: Good measuring
items: Leaving gaps between steps gives a correct count.
Gaps make the count too small.
Line up one end of each string to compare.
Then the other ends show which is longest.
Using a stick again and again needs a mark where it ends each time.
Then there is no overlap or gap.

quiz.q: What is the best way to compare paper strings?
options: Line up one end of each and see where the other ends are
quiz.explain: Matching one end shows clearly which is longest.
steps: To compare strings, start them at the same line.
Then see where the other ends are.
Answer: Line up one end of each and see where the other ends are
quiz.mistake: Does not line up the ends

quiz.q: Rohit walks heel to toe across the room: 20 steps. Asha walks with big gaps: 14 steps. Whose count is better?
options: Rohit's, as there are no gaps
quiz.explain: Heel-to-toe has no gaps, so it measures correctly.
steps: A good method has no gaps and no overlaps.
Heel to toe has no gaps. Big gaps miss some length.
Answer: Rohit's, as there are no gaps
quiz.mistake: Thinks the smaller count is better

quiz.q: A rope fits 6 times between two walls. Another rope twice as long would fit how many times?
quiz.explain: A longer rope fits fewer times: 6 ÷ 2 = 3.
steps: A longer unit fits fewer times.
Twice as long → half as many times.

quiz.q: A board border needs 5 strings on the top, 5 on the bottom and 3 on each side. How many strings?
Which method gives the SAME answer for everyone measuring a wall?
quiz.explain: Everyone using the same stick gets the same count.
steps: Footsteps and hand spans are different for each person.
If everyone uses the same stick, they get the same count.
quiz.mistake: Thinks body units are the same for all

quiz.q: Strings: red 7 spans, blue 4 spans, green 9 spans. Which is shortest?
quiz.explain: 4 spans is the smallest.

quiz.q: Same strings (7, 4, 9 spans). How many spans longer is green than blue?
Ram lays a stick 8 times along a wall but the stick overlaps a bit each time. Is the real length more or less than 8 sticks?
quiz.explain: Overlaps mean each stick covers less new wall, so 8 sticks cover less than 8 full lengths. The wall is less than 8 sticks long.

teach.ask: Gappu wants to measure his branch with a twig. What should he be careful about?
teach.praise: No gaps, no overlaps, same twig every time! Chirp!
teach.nudge: What happens if I leave gaps?

revise.summary: To measure a distance, lay a unit again and again with no gaps and no overlaps. To compare strings, line up one end of each.
focus: Measure without gaps or overlaps.
Compare strings from the same start line.
Count strings around a border.
remember: Use the same unit every time.
A rope twice as long fits half as many times.
traps: Don't leave gaps between steps.
Line up the ends before comparing.
Count all four sides of a border.

learn.hook: Cut a thread exactly as long as this line. Not longer, not shorter!
points: To cut a thread as long as a line, lay it along the line from one end to the other and cut where the line ends.
To draw a string longer than a given one, go past its end. Shorter? Stop before the end.
To complete the other half of a moustache, make it the same length as the first half.
To choose the longest string, compare directly: put them side by side with the ends matching.

example.q: One half of a drawn moustache is 3 boxes long. How long should the other half be?

learn.reallife: Tailors match sleeve lengths so both sleeves of a kurta are equal.

games.title: Match it
items: To match a line, start the thread at one end of the line.
Then cut at the other end.
A longer string goes past the end of the given one.
Both halves of a moustache can be different lengths.
To compare, ends must be lined up.

games.title: Longer or shorter than a 5-box line?

quiz.q: A line is 6 boxes long. Which thread matches it?
quiz.explain: Same length means same number of boxes.
steps: A thread that matches must also be 6 boxes.

quiz.q: Draw a string longer than a 4-box string. How many boxes could it be?
quiz.explain: 6 is more than 4.
steps: Longer than 4 boxes means more than 4.

quiz.q: Draw a string shorter than an 8-box string. How many boxes could it be?
quiz.explain: 5 is less than 8.
steps: Shorter than 8 boxes means less than 8.

quiz.q: A moustache's left half is 4 boxes. The right half is 3 boxes. How many boxes must be added to the right?
steps: Both halves must match. Left = 4 boxes, right = 3 boxes.

quiz.q: Three strings are lined up at one end. Red ends at 9, blue at 12, green at 10. Which is longest?
quiz.explain: 12 goes furthest.
steps: The strings start at the same end.
Red ends at 9, blue at 12, green at 10.

quiz.q: A full moustache has two equal halves of 5 boxes each. How many boxes long is it in all?
Mohan starts his thread a little after the start of the line and cuts at the end of the line. His thread is…
quiz.explain: He started late, so his thread misses a bit at the start.
steps: The thread must start where the line starts.
Mohan started a little after the start.
So his thread misses a bit and is shorter.
quiz.mistake: Does not notice the late start

quiz.q: Raju's string is 3 boxes longer than a 6-box string. How many boxes long is Raju's string?
steps: Raju's string is 3 boxes longer than 6 boxes.

teach.ask: Gappu needs a worm exactly as long as his twig. How should he check?
teach.praise: Put them side by side, ends together. If they end at the same place, they match! Chirp!
teach.nudge: Where should the two start?

revise.summary: To match a length, lay the thread from one end of the line to the other. To draw longer, go past the end; shorter, stop before it.
focus: Cut a thread to match a line.
Draw longer and shorter strings.
Complete equal halves.
remember: Both halves of a moustache are the same length.
traps: Start at the very beginning of the line.
Longer means more boxes, not equal.
Don't add both halves when asked how many to add.

learn.hook: Will the big table fit through the door? We cannot lift it to try. Use a string!
points: When two things cannot be placed side by side, use a third thing, like a string or stick.
Measure the table's width with a string and mark it. Then hold the same string against the door.
If the door is wider than the string mark, the table will fit.
Build a block bridge, measure the gap under it, and guess which toys will pass under.
A tall truck or a long ladder held upright may not pass through a school gate.

example.q: A string matches the width of a cupboard. When held across a door, the string is longer than the door is wide. Will the cupboard pass?
steps: The cupboard is as wide as the string.
The door is narrower than the string.

learn.reallife: Before buying a sofa or a fridge, families measure the door to check that it will fit through!

games.title: Indirect comparison
items: A string can carry a length from one place to another.
We must always lift things to compare them.
A string or stick can help.
If the string is shorter than the gap, the object can pass.
A bridge 4 blocks high lets a 6-block toy pass under it.

quiz.q: How can you compare the width of a table and a door without moving the table?
options: Use a string to measure one and compare with the other
quiz.explain: The string carries the length across.
steps: The table cannot be moved to the door.
Measure the table with a string and mark it.
Hold the same string against the door to compare.
Answer: Use a string to measure one and compare with the other
quiz.mistake: Thinks you must move the table

quiz.q: The string for the table is shorter than the door's width. What does this tell us?
quiz.explain: The door is wider than the table.
steps: The string is as wide as the table.
The string is shorter than the door's width.
So the door is wider than the table.

quiz.q: A bridge has a gap 5 blocks high. A toy is 3 blocks tall. Can it pass?
quiz.explain: 3 is less than 5, so it fits under.
steps: Gap = 5 blocks high. Toy = 3 blocks tall.

quiz.q: A gap under the bridge is 4 blocks high. Which toy CANNOT pass?
quiz.explain: 6 is more than 4.
steps: Toys of 1, 2 and 3 blocks are less than 4.

quiz.q: A pole is 7 sticks tall and the gate is 5 sticks tall. How many sticks too tall is the pole to pass standing up?
Which might NOT pass through a school gate?
quiz.explain: A truck is too tall and wide for most school gates.
steps: A bicycle, a child and a bag are small.
A big truck is too tall and wide for most school gates.

quiz.q: Raju's string matches his window's width. It is longer than Mira's window. Whose window is wider?
quiz.explain: Raju's window is as wide as the string, and the string is longer than Mira's window.
steps: The string is longer than Mira's window.

quiz.q: Why do we need a third object like a string?
options: When two things cannot be put side by side
quiz.explain: It lets us compare lengths in different places.
steps: Sometimes two things cannot be put side by side.
A string carries the length from one place to the other.
Answer: When two things cannot be put side by side

teach.ask: Gappu wants to know if his nest will fit in a hole in the tree. He cannot carry the nest. What can he do?
teach.praise: Measure the nest with a grass blade, then hold it at the hole! Chirp!
teach.nudge: What can I carry to the hole instead of the nest?

revise.summary: When two things cannot be placed side by side, use a third thing like a string to carry the length across and compare.
focus: Compare with a string or stick.
Decide if something will fit through a gap.
Find how much too tall something is.
remember: If the door is wider than the string mark, the table will fit.
A 3-block toy passes under a 5-block gap.
A pole of 7 sticks is 2 too tall for a 5-stick gate.
traps: You don't need to move the table to compare.
Don't reverse the comparison.
A third object is for comparing, not decoration.

learn.hook: Is your arm span the same as your height? Let us test it like scientists!
points: Some body measures are often close to each other. We test them to see if they are true for everyone.
Test 1: wrap a string around your head. Is it about 3 of your hand spans?
Test 2: is your forearm (elbow to wrist) about as long as your foot?
Test 3: stretch your arms wide. Is your arm span about the same as your height?
Test many people and record 'yes' or 'no'. If even one person does not fit, it is not true for ALL.

example.q: 8 friends test arm span = height. 7 say yes and 1 says no. Is it true for all?
example.answer: No, it is true for most but not all

learn.reallife: Artists drawing people use body measures like these to get the shape right.

games.title: Testing ideas
items: To test an idea, we try it on many people.
If one person does not fit, it is not true for all.
We can test arm span with a string.
Measure the span and then compare with height.
Testing only yourself proves it for everyone.

quiz.q: How can you test if your arm span equals your height?
options: Measure both with a string and compare
quiz.explain: A string shows both lengths so you can compare them.
steps: Answer: Measure both with a string and compare

quiz.q: How can you check if your head is about 3 hand spans around?
options: Wrap a string around your head and measure it in spans
quiz.explain: The string gives the distance around, and then we measure it with spans.
steps: Answer: Wrap a string around your head and measure it in spans

quiz.q: Forearm means…
quiz.explain: The forearm is the part from the elbow to the wrist.
steps: The forearm is part of the arm.
It goes from the elbow to the wrist.
Shoulder to elbow is the upper arm.

quiz.q: 15 children test 'forearm = foot'. 12 say yes. How many say no?
In the test above, is 'forearm = foot' true for ALL 15 children?
quiz.explain: All means every one. 3 did not fit.
steps: 'True for all' means every one fits.
So it is not true for all, only for most.

quiz.q: Riya's head is 3 spans around. Her brother's head is also 3 of HIS spans. Are their heads the same size?
options: Not necessarily: their spans may be different
quiz.explain: 3 spans each, but spans are different sizes.
steps: Each head is 3 spans, but each used their own span.
So we cannot say the heads are the same size.
Answer: Not necessarily: their spans may be different
quiz.mistake: Thinks spans are the same for all

quiz.q: Which is the best way to test an idea about body measures?
options: Try it on many people and record
quiz.explain: Many people give a fairer answer.
steps: One person or a guess is not enough.
Testing many people and recording gives a fairer answer.
Answer: Try it on many people and record

quiz.q: 6 friends tested arm span = height. All 6 said yes. Can we be sure it is true for every person in the world?
quiz.explain: It is true for these 6, but other people may be different.
steps: So we cannot be sure for everyone.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a small test proves it for all

teach.ask: Gappu says 'My wings are as long as my body, so it is true for all birds!' What would you tell him?
teach.praise: I should test many birds before I say ALL! Chirp!
teach.nudge: Is one bird enough to be sure?

revise.summary: Some body measures are close to each other, like arm span and height. We test many people to see if an idea is true for all.
focus: Test body measure ideas on many people.
Count yes and no answers.
Decide if an idea is true for all.
remember: Head around ≈ 3 hand spans. Forearm (elbow to wrist) ≈ foot.
If even one person does not fit, it is not true for all.
traps: 'Most' does not mean 'all'.
A small test does not prove it for everyone.
The forearm is elbow to wrist, not shoulder to elbow.

learn.hook: Hand spans gave everyone a different answer. The metre gives everyone the SAME answer!
points: We need a standard unit so that everyone gets the same measure.
The metre (m) is a standard unit of length. A metre rod or a measuring tape shows 1 metre.
Make a one-metre rope: lay a rope along a metre rod and cut it at the end.
Mark 1 metre from the floor on a wall. Stand against it to see if you are taller or shorter than 1 metre.
A door is about 2 metres tall. A classroom may be about 6 to 8 metres long.

example.q: A rope is laid along a metre rod 3 times to measure a mat. How long is the mat?

learn.reallife: Cloth shops sell cloth by the metre, and sports tracks are measured in metres.

games.title: Metre facts
items: A metre is a standard unit of length.
It is the same for everyone.
A hand span is a standard unit.
Hand spans differ from person to person.
A measuring tape can show 1 metre.

items.q: Mat 2 m, 3 mats in a row

quiz.q: Why do we need a standard unit like the metre?
options: So everyone gets the same measure
quiz.explain: Body units differ, but a metre is the same for all.
steps: Body units differ from person to person.
A metre is the same for everyone.
So a standard unit gives everyone the same measure.
Answer: So everyone gets the same measure

quiz.q: Which tool shows 1 metre?
quiz.explain: A metre rod is exactly 1 metre long.
steps: A spoon, a clock and a balance do not measure length in metres.
A metre rod is exactly 1 metre long.
quiz.mistake: Picks a tool for weight or time

quiz.q: How do you make a 1-metre rope?
options: Lay it along a metre rod and cut at the end
quiz.explain: Matching it to the metre rod makes it exactly 1 metre.
steps: Lay the rope along a metre rod.
Cut it where the rod ends.
Now the rope is exactly 1 metre.
Answer: Lay it along a metre rod and cut at the end

quiz.q: A mat is 2 m long. Three mats in a row are how long?
steps: Each mat = 2 m. 3 mats in a row.

quiz.q: Ravi stands against a 1-metre mark on the wall. His head is above the mark. What does this tell us?
quiz.explain: Above the mark means taller.
steps: Ravi's head is above the 1-metre mark.
Answer: Ravi is taller than 1 metre

quiz.q: A rope is 5 m long. 2 m is cut off. How much is left?
Which is about 1 metre long?
options: A big stride of a grown-up
quiz.explain: A big stride is about 1 metre.
steps: A pencil and an ant are too short. A cricket ground is far too long.
A big stride of a grown-up is about 1 metre.
Answer: A big stride of a grown-up
quiz.mistake: Picks something too short or too long

quiz.q: Tina measures her room with a metre tape: 4 m. Her friend measures it with the same tape. What will the friend get?
quiz.explain: A standard unit gives the same answer for everyone.
steps: A metre tape is a standard unit.
A standard unit gives the same answer for everyone.
So the friend also gets 4 m.
quiz.mistake: Thinks results differ like hand spans

teach.ask: Gappu asks why we use metres and not wing lengths. What would you tell him?
teach.praise: A metre is the same for everyone, but wings are different! Chirp!
teach.nudge: Is a wing length the same for every bird?

revise.summary: The metre (m) is a standard unit of length. Everyone who uses a metre gets the same measure.
focus: Explain why we need a standard unit.
Make a 1-metre rope.
Add and take away lengths in metres.
remember: A metre rod or tape shows 1 metre.
A door is about 2 m tall. A big stride is about 1 m.
3 lays of a metre rope = 3 m.
traps: Body units are not the same for all. Metres are.
Above the 1 m mark means taller, not shorter.
The same tape gives the same answer for everyone.

learn.hook: Is your friend taller than a metre rod? Is a door? Is a pencil? Let us sort!
points: Stand friends next to a 1-metre mark. Sort them: taller than 1 m, or shorter than 1 m.
Many Class 3 children are a little taller than 1 metre.
Objects can be longer than, shorter than or about equal to 1 metre.
Longer than 1 m: a door, a bed, a classroom. Shorter: a pencil, a book, a shoe. About 1 m: a metre rod, a big stride.

example.q: Sort: bed, eraser, metre rod.
steps: A bed is long: longer than 1 m.
A metre rod is exactly 1 m.
example.answer: Longer: bed; shorter: eraser; equal: metre rod

learn.reallife: At amusement parks, some rides have a height mark. You must be taller than it to ride!

items.q: Taller 9, shorter 6. How many more taller?

quiz.q: Which is longer than 1 metre?
quiz.explain: A door is about 2 metres tall.
steps: A pencil, a shoe and a spoon are shorter than 1 m.
A door is about 2 metres tall.

quiz.q: Which is shorter than 1 metre?
quiz.explain: A notebook is much shorter than a metre.
steps: A bus, a bed and a classroom are longer than 1 m.
A notebook is much shorter than 1 metre.

quiz.q: Which is about 1 metre?
quiz.explain: A metre rod is exactly 1 metre.
steps: A house and a train are much longer. An eraser is much shorter.
A metre rod is exactly 1 metre.

quiz.q: In a class, 18 children are taller than 1 m and 7 are shorter. How many children?
Same class: how many more are taller than 1 m than shorter?
Ajay's head is below the 1-metre mark. He is…
quiz.explain: Below the mark means shorter.
steps: Ajay's head is below the 1-metre mark.

quiz.q: A bed is about 2 m long. Is that more or less than 1 metre?
quiz.explain: 2 metres is more than 1 metre.

quiz.q: Which list has ONLY things longer than 1 metre?
quiz.explain: A bus, a door and a bed are all longer than 1 m.
steps: Pencil, shoe, book, eraser, spoon and cup are shorter than 1 m.
Bus, door and bed are all longer than 1 m.

teach.ask: Gappu wants to sort his friends by height using 1 metre. How should he do it?
teach.praise: Make a 1-metre mark, then sort: above it is taller, below is shorter! Chirp!
teach.nudge: What should I compare each friend with?

revise.summary: Objects and people can be longer than, shorter than or about 1 metre. A 1-metre mark on a wall helps us sort.
focus: Sort objects as longer, shorter or about 1 m.
Sort friends against a 1-metre mark.
Add and compare the counts.
remember: Longer than 1 m: door, bed, classroom.
Shorter than 1 m: pencil, book, shoe.
About 1 m: metre rod, big stride.
traps: Below the mark means shorter.
2 m is more than 1 m.
Check every item in a list.

learn.hook: Fold a 1-metre rope in half. Now you have a half-metre! Fold again for a quarter-metre!
points: Fold a 1-metre rope in half and cut: each piece is half a metre.
Fold the half-metre in half again: each piece is a quarter metre.
2 half metres make 1 metre. 4 quarter metres make 1 metre. 2 quarter metres make a half metre.
Sort objects: less than a quarter metre (an eraser), about half a metre (a school bag), about 1 metre.
Measure a long jump with a metre rope: 1 metre and a half metre is one and a half metres.

example.q: Leela jumps 1 metre rope + 1 half-metre rope + 1 quarter-metre rope. How far?
steps: 1 m + half m = one and a half m

learn.reallife: Cloth shops sell half a metre or a quarter metre of ribbon too.

quiz.q: How do you make a half-metre rope from a 1-metre rope?
options: Fold it in half and cut
quiz.explain: Folding in half gives two equal halves.
steps: Each piece is half a metre.
Answer: Fold it in half and cut

quiz.q: How many half metres make 1 metre?
quiz.explain: 2 halves make a whole.

quiz.q: How many quarter metres make 1 metre?
quiz.explain: 4 quarters make a whole.

quiz.q: How many quarter metres make a half metre?
quiz.explain: 2 quarters = 1 half.
steps: A quarter metre is half of a half metre.
So 2 quarter metres make a half metre.

quiz.q: Which is about half a metre long?
quiz.explain: A school bag is about half a metre tall.
steps: A pin and an ant are tiny. A bus is very long.
A school bag is about half a metre.

quiz.q: Which is LESS than a quarter metre?
quiz.explain: An eraser is very small.
steps: A bicycle, a door and a bed are long.
An eraser is very small, less than a quarter metre.

quiz.q: A throw is measured with 3 metre ropes and 1 half-metre rope. How far?
quiz.explain: 3 m + half m = 3 and a half m.
steps: 3 m + half m = 3 and a half metres.
quiz.mistake: Counts the half rope as a full metre

quiz.q: A ribbon is 4 quarter metres long. How long is it?
quiz.explain: 4 quarters make 1 whole metre.

teach.ask: Gappu has a 1-metre vine. How can he get a quarter-metre piece?
teach.praise: Fold in half, then fold in half again: a quarter metre! Chirp!
teach.nudge: How many folds do I need?

revise.summary: Fold a 1-metre rope in half to get half metres, and in half again to get quarter metres.
focus: Make half and quarter metres.
Know how many halves and quarters make a metre.
Measure with metres and parts of metres.
remember: 2 half metres = 1 metre. 4 quarter metres = 1 metre.
3 m and a half m = 3 and a half metres.
traps: Folding once gives halves, not quarters.
A half-metre rope is not a full metre.
4 quarter metres is 1 metre, not 4 metres.

learn.hook: Close your eyes and cut a thread you think is 1 metre long. Now check with a metre rod. How close were you?
points: Estimate 1 metre by cutting a thread, then check it with a metre rod.
To cut a rope into 4 equal pieces, you need only 3 cuts.
In general, the number of cuts is one less than the number of pieces.
Count how many of your footsteps make 1 metre. It may be 4 or 5 for a child.
Measure a classroom wall with a metre rope: lay it end to end and count.

example.q: How many cuts are needed to cut a ribbon into 6 equal pieces?

learn.reallife: A carpenter cutting a plank into pieces must plan the number of cuts, not just the pieces.

games.title: Metre fun facts
items: Checking an estimate with a metre rod shows how close we were.
Everyone takes the same number of footsteps for 1 metre.
Laying a metre rope 5 times along a wall means the wall is about 5 m.

quiz.q: How many cuts make 4 equal pieces of a rope?
quiz.explain: Pieces − 1 = cuts. 4 − 1 = 3.

quiz.q: How many pieces do 2 cuts make?
quiz.explain: Cuts + 1 = pieces.

quiz.q: Sita's guessed thread is a bit longer than the metre rod. What was her estimate?
quiz.explain: Longer than the rod means more than 1 m.
steps: Sita's thread is a bit longer than the metre rod.
Longer than 1 m means more than 1 metre.

quiz.q: Kabir takes 5 footsteps to cover 1 metre. How many footsteps for 3 metres?
A metre rope is laid along a wall 8 times. How long is the wall?
quiz.explain: Each lay is 1 metre: 8 × 1 = 8 m.
steps: Each lay of the rope is 1 metre.

quiz.q: Why might Ria and her teacher take different numbers of steps to make 1 metre?
quiz.explain: Bigger steps mean fewer steps.
steps: Ria's steps and her teacher's steps are different sizes.
Answer: Their steps are different sizes

quiz.q: A ribbon is cut into 10 equal pieces. How many cuts?
Raju's estimate of 1 metre was exactly as long as the metre rod. What does this mean?
quiz.explain: Same length as the rod means exactly 1 metre.
steps: Raju's thread was exactly as long as the metre rod.

teach.ask: Gappu wants to cut a worm-shaped noodle into 5 equal pieces. How many cuts must he make?
teach.praise: 4 cuts give 5 pieces: one less cut than pieces! Chirp!
teach.nudge: For 2 pieces, how many cuts do I need?

revise.summary: Estimate 1 metre and check with a metre rod. To cut something into equal pieces, the cuts are one less than the pieces.
focus: Estimate and check 1 metre.
Find the number of cuts for some pieces.
Count footsteps for a metre.
remember: A child may take 4 or 5 footsteps for 1 metre.
traps: Cuts are not equal to pieces.
10 pieces need 9 cuts, not 10.
The metre does not change. Step sizes do.

learn.hook: 2, 4, 6, 8... who do we appreciate? Number patterns, of course!
points: A pattern follows a rule again and again.
Some patterns grow by adding: 2, 4, 6, 8 (add 2 each time).
Some patterns get smaller by taking away: 50, 45, 40 (take away 5 each time).
Find the rule by looking at how each number changes to the next.
Even numbers end in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8. Odd numbers end in 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9. They take turns: even, odd, even, odd.

example.q: What comes next: 3, 7, 11, 15, ___?

learn.reallife: House numbers on one side of a street often go 2, 4, 6, 8 and on the other side 1, 3, 5, 7.

quiz.q: What comes next? 5, 10, 15, 20, ___
quiz.explain: The rule is 'add 5'. 20 + 5 = 25.

quiz.q: What is the rule? 30, 27, 24, 21
quiz.explain: Each number is 3 less than the one before: 30 − 3 = 27, 27 − 3 = 24.
quiz.mistake: Sees a jump of 3 but misses that the numbers are getting smaller

quiz.q: Find the missing number: 6, 12, ___, 24, 30
quiz.explain: The rule is 'add 6'. 12 + 6 = 18, and 18 + 6 = 24.
quiz.mistake: Uses a jump of 2 or 4 instead of 6

quiz.q: What comes next? 1, 4, 7, 10, ___
quiz.explain: The rule is 'add 3'. 10 + 3 = 13.

quiz.q: Which number is EVEN?
quiz.explain: Even numbers end in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8. 58 ends in 8.
steps: 37, 45 and 91 end in 7, 5 and 1. They are odd.
quiz.mistake: Looks at the tens digit instead of the ones digit

quiz.q: At the party, Riya puts 2 balloons on the first chair, 4 on the second and 6 on the third. How many on the fourth chair?
quiz.explain: The rule is 'add 2'. 6 + 2 = 8.

quiz.q: What comes next? 50, 40, 30, ___
quiz.explain: The rule is 'take away 10'. 30 − 10 = 20.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the pattern goes up instead of down

quiz.q: Arjun's pattern is 2, 4, 8, 16, ___. Each number is double the one before. What comes next?
quiz.explain: Double 16 is 16 + 16 = 32.
steps: Rule: each number is double the one before.
quiz.mistake: Adds 2 each time instead of doubling

teach.ask: Gappu sees 4, 8, 12, 16 on the party board. How can he find the next number?
teach.praise: Add 4 each time! The next number is 20!
teach.nudge: How does each number change to the next one?

revise.summary: A number pattern follows a rule again and again, like add 2 or take away 5. Find the rule by seeing how each number changes.
focus: Find the rule of a pattern.
Find the next or missing number.
Tell even and odd numbers.
remember: Even numbers end in 0, 2, 4, 6, 8. Odd end in 1, 3, 5, 7, 9.
traps: Check if the pattern goes up or down.
Don't add 1 when the jump is bigger.
Doubling is not adding 2.

learn.hook: Party flags, bangles and rangoli all have patterns. Can you guess what comes next?
points: A repeating pattern has a part that comes again and again: 🔴🔵🔴🔵.
The part that repeats is called the core. In red, blue, blue, red, blue, blue, the core is red, blue, blue.
A growing pattern gets bigger at each step: 1 dot, 2 dots, 3 dots.
To find what comes next, find the core or the rule first.

example.q: Party flags go: green, yellow, yellow, green, yellow, yellow, ___. What comes next?
steps: The core is green, yellow, yellow.
After the second yellow, the core starts again.

learn.reallife: Borders of saris, bead necklaces and paper chains for parties all show patterns.

items.text: A, B, B, A, B, B, ___

games.title: Pattern detective
items: Red, blue, red, blue is a repeating pattern.
Red, blue comes again and again.
A growing pattern gets bigger at each step.
In red, white, red, white ..., the 6th bead is white.
Red is in places 1, 3, 5. White is in places 2, 4, 6.
Circle, square, circle, square ...: the 5th shape is a square.

quiz.q: What comes next? 🔴🟢🔴🟢🔴___
quiz.explain: The core is 🔴🟢. After 🔴 comes 🟢.
quiz.mistake: Repeats the last colour instead of following the core

quiz.q: Bangles go: red, red, gold, red, red, gold. What is the core of this pattern?
quiz.explain: The part that repeats is red, red, gold.
steps: Look for the part that repeats.
red, red, gold | red, red, gold
The core is red, red, gold.
quiz.mistake: Misses one of the reds in the core

quiz.q: Rangoli dots go: 1 dot, 3 dots, 5 dots, 7 dots. How many dots come next?
quiz.explain: Each step adds 2 dots. 7 + 2 = 9.

quiz.q: A paper chain goes pink, blue, pink, blue ... What colour is the 8th ring?
quiz.explain: Pink is in places 1, 3, 5, 7. Blue is in places 2, 4, 6, 8. So the 8th ring is blue.

quiz.q: Which of these is a GROWING pattern?
quiz.explain: In ⭐, ⭐⭐, ⭐⭐⭐ each step has one more star, so it grows.
steps: A growing pattern gets bigger at each step.
⭐, ⭐⭐, ⭐⭐⭐ has one more star each step.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up repeating patterns with growing patterns

quiz.q: Kabir sets plates: big, small, small, big, small, small, big, ___. What comes next?
quiz.explain: The core is big, small, small. After 'big' comes 'small'.
steps: The core is big, small, small.
big, small, small | big, small, small | big, ___
quiz.mistake: Thinks the pattern just takes turns, big then small then big

quiz.q: Tiles: step 1 has 2 tiles, step 2 has 4 tiles, step 3 has 6 tiles. How many tiles in step 4?
quiz.explain: Each step adds 2 tiles. 6 + 2 = 8.

quiz.q: A border goes triangle, circle, square, triangle, circle, square ... Which shape is 7th?
quiz.explain: The core has 3 shapes. Places 1, 4 and 7 are triangles.

teach.ask: Gappu made a necklace: red bead, yellow bead, yellow bead, red bead, yellow bead... What bead comes next and how do you know?
teach.praise: Red, yellow, yellow keeps repeating, so yellow comes next! My necklace looks lovely.
teach.nudge: Which part of my necklace keeps coming again?

revise.summary: A repeating pattern has a core that comes again and again. A growing pattern gets bigger at each step.
focus: Find the core of a repeating pattern.
Find what comes next.
Tell repeating and growing patterns apart.
remember: Core of red, blue, blue, red, blue, blue is red, blue, blue.
traps: Don't just repeat the last item. Follow the core.
Count every item in the core.
A repeating pattern is not a growing pattern.

learn.hook: Fold a paper butterfly down the middle. Both wings match perfectly. That's symmetry!
points: A shape is symmetrical if one half is a mirror image of the other half.
The fold line that makes two matching halves is called the line of symmetry.
Letters like A, H, M, O, T, U, V, W, X and Y have matching halves when folded along a standing line down the middle.
Some shapes have more than one line of symmetry. A square has 4. A circle has many.
Rangoli and kolam designs are often symmetrical.

example.q: How many lines of symmetry does a long rectangle, like a door, have?
steps: Fold it along a standing line down the middle: the halves match.
Fold it along a sleeping line across the middle: the halves match.
Fold it corner to corner: the halves do NOT match.

learn.reallife: Butterflies, leaves, diyas, the Taj Mahal and many rangoli designs are symmetrical.

games.title: Mirror, mirror
items: A square has 4 lines of symmetry.
2 folds through the middle of the sides and 2 folds corner to corner.
No fold makes the two halves of F match.
A circle has many lines of symmetry.
Any fold through the centre makes two matching halves.
A long rectangle, like a door, has 4 lines of symmetry.
It has only 2. Corner-to-corner folds do not match.
The two halves of a symmetrical shape match exactly.

quiz.q: What do we call the fold line that splits a shape into two matching halves?
quiz.explain: A line of symmetry divides a shape into two halves that are mirror images.
steps: The fold line makes two matching halves.
This line is called the line of symmetry.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the line of symmetry with the edge of the shape

quiz.q: Which letter is symmetrical?
quiz.explain: Fold H down the middle and both halves match. F, G and R do not have matching halves.
steps: Fold each letter down the middle in your mind.
F, G and R do not have matching halves.
quiz.mistake: Picks a letter without trying to fold it in the mind

quiz.q: How many lines of symmetry does a square have?
quiz.explain: A square can be folded top to bottom, side to side and along both corner-to-corner lines. That makes 4.

quiz.q: Riya folds a paper heart down the middle and the two halves match. The heart is ___.
quiz.explain: When two halves match exactly after folding, the shape is symmetrical.
steps: The two halves match exactly after folding.
A shape like this is symmetrical.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect matching halves with symmetry

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT symmetrical?
quiz.explain: J has a hook on one side only, so no fold makes its halves match.
steps: A, a butterfly and O have matching halves.
J has a hook on one side only.
No fold makes its halves match.
quiz.mistake: Misses the word NOT in the question

quiz.q: How many lines of symmetry does a long rectangle, like a door, have?
quiz.explain: Folding down the middle and across the middle both work. Corner-to-corner folds do not.
steps: Corner to corner: does not match
quiz.mistake: Thinks a rectangle has 4 lines like a square

quiz.q: Aisha drew half of a rangoli flower. To make it symmetrical, the other half must be ___.
options: a mirror copy of the first half
quiz.explain: In a symmetrical design, one half is a mirror image of the other.
steps: In a symmetrical design, one half is a mirror image of the other.
So the other half must be a mirror copy.
Answer: a mirror copy of the first half
quiz.mistake: Thinks symmetry means just filling the space

quiz.q: Which word is made ONLY of letters that match when folded down the middle?
quiz.explain: T, O, M and A all match when folded down the middle. MANGO has N and G, CAKE has C, K and E, PIZZA has P and Z. These do not.
steps: Check every letter folded down the middle.
T, O, M and A all match, so TOMATO works.
MANGO has N, G. CAKE has C, K, E. PIZZA has P, Z.
quiz.mistake: Checks only some of the letters

teach.ask: Gappu found a butterfly and a leaf. His friend says they are symmetrical. What does that mean?
teach.praise: Fold it in the middle and both halves match! Butterflies are symmetrical!
teach.nudge: What happens to the two halves when I fold it down the middle?

revise.summary: A shape is symmetrical if one half is a mirror image of the other. The fold line is the line of symmetry.
focus: Find symmetrical letters and shapes.
Count lines of symmetry.
Complete a symmetrical design.
remember: A, H, M, O, T, U, V, W, X, Y match when folded down the middle.
A square has 4 lines of symmetry. A circle has many.
A long rectangle has 2 lines of symmetry.
traps: A rectangle does not have 4 lines like a square.
The line of symmetry is not the edge.
Read NOT in the question.

learn.hook: Chintu fills a bucket with a big glass. Mintu uses a small glass. Who needs more glasses?
points: A bigger glass holds more, so FEWER big glasses fill a bucket.
A smaller glass holds less, so MORE small glasses are needed.
To compare two containers, fill each and pour into same-sized glasses. The one that fills more glasses holds more.
Use words: holds more, holds less, holds the most, holds the least.

example.q: A jug fills 6 glasses. A bottle fills 4 of the same glasses. Which holds more?

learn.reallife: At a wedding, big pots of water are poured into small glasses to serve guests.

games.title: Least to most
games.prompt: Each fills this many same glasses: cup 1, bottle 3, jug 5, bucket 20

games.title: More or less?
items: A bigger glass needs fewer fills.
Containers that look tall always hold more.
A tall thin glass may hold less than a wide bowl.
Pouring into same-sized glasses is a fair way to compare.
The same unit is used for both.
The container that fills the fewest glasses holds the most.

quiz.q: Chintu's glass is bigger than Mintu's. Who needs fewer glasses to fill a bucket?
quiz.explain: A bigger glass holds more, so fewer are needed.
steps: Chintu's glass is bigger, so it holds more each time.
A bigger glass needs fewer fills to fill the bucket.

quiz.q: A pot fills 8 glasses. A jug fills 5 of the same glasses. How many more glasses does the pot fill?
Bottle A fills 7 cups, bottle B fills 9 cups and bottle C fills 4 cups. Which holds the MOST?
quiz.explain: 9 cups is the most.
steps: A 7 cups, B 9 cups, C 4 cups.
B fills the most cups, so it holds the most.

quiz.q: Same bottles (7, 9, 4 cups). Which holds the LEAST?
quiz.explain: 4 cups is the least.
steps: A 7 cups, B 9 cups, C 4 cups.

quiz.q: To compare a bottle and a jug fairly, what should we pour them into?
quiz.explain: The same-sized glass is a fair unit.
steps: To compare fairly, use the same unit for both.
So pour both into glasses of the same size.
Answer: Glasses of the same size

quiz.q: A tank fills 20 big buckets or 40 small buckets. Which bucket holds more?
quiz.explain: Fewer big buckets are needed, so each holds more.
steps: The tank needs 20 big buckets or 40 small buckets.
Fewer big buckets are needed, so each big bucket holds more.

quiz.q: A tall, thin glass and a short, wide bowl. How can we be sure which holds more?
options: Fill one and pour into the other
quiz.explain: Pouring tests it. Height alone can fool us.
steps: Fill one and pour it into the other.
If it overflows, the first holds more.
Answer: Fill one and pour into the other

quiz.q: Jug fills 6 glasses. Pot fills twice as many. How many glasses does the pot fill?
steps: Jug = 6 glasses. Pot = twice as many.

teach.ask: Gappu has a big leaf cup and a small leaf cup. Which fills the pond bowl with fewer trips?
teach.praise: The big cup holds more, so I need fewer trips! Chirp!
teach.nudge: Which cup holds more each time?

revise.summary: A bigger glass holds more, so fewer big glasses fill a bucket. To compare containers fairly, pour each into same-sized glasses.
focus: Compare containers by counting same-sized glasses.
Use holds more, less, most and least.
Know that bigger units need fewer fills.
remember: Bigger glass → fewer fills. Smaller glass → more fills.
Jug 6 glasses, bottle 4 glasses: the jug holds more.
traps: More fills does not mean the glass is bigger.
Don't use glasses of different sizes to compare.
Height alone does not tell which holds more.

learn.hook: A bucket or a cup: which one would you use to fill a bathtub? Let's compare how much things hold!
points: Capacity is how much a container can hold.
We can compare by filling one container and pouring it into another.
We can measure with small cups or glasses: a jug may hold 6 glasses of water.
Litre (L) is the standard unit for liquids like milk, water and oil.
Small amounts are measured in millilitres (mL). 1 litre = 1000 millilitres.

example.q: A bucket holds 10 mugs of water. A pot holds 4 mugs. How many more mugs does the bucket hold?

learn.reallife: Milk comes in 1 litre and half-litre packets, and water bottles are often 1 litre.

games.title: Less or more than a litre?
Little to large
games.prompt: Holds the least to holds the most

quiz.q: Which of these holds the MOST water?
quiz.explain: A bucket is much bigger inside than a cup, spoon or glass, so it holds the most.
steps: A spoon, a cup and a glass are small.
A bucket is much bigger inside.

quiz.q: Which unit do we use to measure milk?
quiz.explain: Liquids like milk are measured in litres.
steps: Kilogram is for weight. Metre is for length.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the unit for weight with the unit for liquids

quiz.q: One jug of water fills 5 glasses. How many glasses do 2 jugs fill?
quiz.explain: 2 jugs fill 5 + 5 = 10 glasses.

quiz.q: How many millilitres are there in 1 litre?
quiz.explain: 1 litre = 1000 millilitres.

quiz.q: Riya's bottle holds 2 litres of water. She drinks 1 litre. How much water is left?
quiz.explain: 2 litres − 1 litre = 1 litre.

quiz.q: A water tank holds 50 buckets of water. 20 buckets are used. How many buckets of water are left?
quiz.explain: 50 − 20 = 30 buckets are left.

quiz.q: Kabir pours a full bottle of water into an empty mug, and the mug overflows. What does this tell us?
options: The mug holds more than the bottle
The bottle holds more than the mug
quiz.explain: The mug could not hold all the water from the bottle, so the bottle holds more.
steps: The full bottle's water does not fit in the mug.
So the mug holds less than the bottle.
Answer: The bottle holds more than the mug
quiz.mistake: Thinks the container that overflows holds more

quiz.q: Half a litre is how many millilitres?
quiz.explain: 1 litre is 1000 mL. Half of 1000 is 500.
quiz.mistake: Thinks 1 litre is 100 mL, so half is 50

teach.ask: Gappu has a cup and a jug. He wants to know which holds more water. How can he find out?
teach.praise: Fill one and pour it into the other! Now I know the jug holds more.
teach.nudge: What can I do with the water to compare them?

revise.summary: Capacity is how much a container can hold. We compare by pouring, measure with cups, and use litres (L) and millilitres (mL).
focus: Compare containers by pouring.
Use litres for liquids.
Know litres and millilitres.
traps: 1 litre is 1000 mL, not 100 mL.
Kilogram is for weight, not liquids.
The container that overflows holds less.

learn.hook: How many ladles of dal fill one glass? Guess first, then pour!
points: Guess how many small containers fill a big one, then check by pouring.
The smaller the measuring vessel, the more times you must fill it.
If 1 jug fills 4 glasses, 3 jugs fill 4 + 4 + 4 = 12 glasses.
If 1 glass takes 5 ladles, 4 glasses take 20 ladles.

example.q: 1 glass takes 3 ladles. How many ladles for 4 glasses?

learn.reallife: In a langar or a school mid-day meal, food is served with ladles of the same size so everyone gets the same.

quiz.q: 1 jug fills 4 glasses. How many glasses do 3 jugs fill?
steps: 1 jug fills 4 glasses. There are 3 jugs.

quiz.q: 1 glass takes 5 ladles. How many ladles for 4 glasses?
steps: 1 glass takes 5 ladles. There are 4 glasses.

quiz.q: A bucket is filled with a mug and with a glass. The glass is smaller. Which needs more fills?
quiz.explain: A smaller vessel needs more fills.
steps: The glass is smaller than the mug.
A smaller vessel needs more fills.
quiz.mistake: Thinks small vessels need fewer fills

quiz.q: Raju guessed 6 cups fill a jug. When he poured, it took 8 cups. How far off was his guess?
Which is best to serve dal at lunch?
quiz.explain: A ladle serves a small amount neatly.
steps: Dal is served in small amounts.
A drum, a tank and a bucket are far too big.
A ladle serves a small amount neatly.

quiz.q: 18 glasses of water are needed. 1 jug fills 6 glasses. How many jugs?
A pot holds 10 bowls of rice. A bowl holds 2 ladles. How many ladles fill the pot?
quiz.explain: 10 bowls × 2 ladles = 20.

quiz.q: Bottle A fills 3 glasses. Bottle B fills 3 cups. Can we say they hold the same?
options: No, glasses and cups may be different sizes
quiz.explain: We can compare only with the same unit.
steps: A was measured in glasses. B was measured in cups.
Glasses and cups may be different sizes.
We can compare only with the same unit.
Answer: No, glasses and cups may be different sizes

teach.ask: Gappu fills his water bowl with a tiny cup and his friend with a big cup. Who pours more times?
teach.praise: The tiny cup holds less, so I pour more times! Chirp!
teach.nudge: Which cup holds less each time?

revise.summary: Guess how many small containers fill a big one, then check by pouring. The smaller the vessel, the more times you fill it.
focus: Find fills using equal groups.
Choose a suitable vessel for a job.
Compare only with the same unit.

learn.hook: Long ago, a farmer swapped rice for a potter's pots. No money at all! Was that easy?
points: Barter means exchanging goods directly: rice for pots, wheat for cloth.
Barter is hard: the potter may not want rice, or 1 pot may be worth less than a sack of rice.
Money solves this. Everyone accepts it, and notes and coins have different values.
We compare costs to see which is cheaper or costlier: a ₹45 book costs more than a ₹30 book.

example.q: A pen costs ₹25 and a pencil box costs ₹60. How much more is the pencil box?

learn.reallife: Even today, people swap things in villages, and children swap stickers. But shops use money.

games.title: Barter or money?
items: Barter means exchanging goods without money.
In barter, both people must want each other's goods.
All notes have the same value.
Money makes buying and selling easier.

quiz.q: What is barter?
quiz.explain: Barter is a direct swap of goods.
steps: No money is used, like rice for pots.

quiz.q: Why is barter difficult?
options: The other person may not want what you have
quiz.explain: Both people must want each other's things.
steps: In barter, both people must want each other's things.

quiz.q: Why do we use money?
options: Everyone accepts it and it has fixed values
quiz.explain: Money is accepted by all and makes trade easy.
steps: Notes and coins have fixed values.
This makes buying and selling easy.

quiz.explain: ₹15 is the least.

revise.summary: Barter means swapping goods without money. It is hard, so we use money, which everyone accepts and which has fixed values.

learn.hook: Jingle, jingle! Coins in your piggy bank and notes in Papa's wallet. How much is it all worth?
points: Indian money is counted in rupees, written as ₹.
Coins come as ₹1, ₹2, ₹5, ₹10 and ₹20.
We can make the same amount in different ways: ₹10 = two ₹5 coins = five ₹2 coins.
To count money, start with the biggest note or coin and count on.

example.q: Aisha has one ₹50 note, two ₹10 notes and one ₹5 coin. How much money does she have?

learn.reallife: Shopkeepers count money every day, starting with the biggest notes first.

quiz.q: Riya has three ₹10 notes. How much money does she have?

quiz.q: How many ₹5 coins make ₹20?

quiz.mistake: Takes away 5 from 20 instead of counting groups of 5

quiz.q: Arjun has one ₹100 note, one ₹20 note and two ₹2 coins. How much money does he have?

steps: Add the value of each group.
quiz.mistake: Counts the coins instead of their value

quiz.q: How many ₹50 notes make ₹200?
quiz.explain: Count by 50s: 50, 100, 150, 200. That is 4 notes.

quiz.q: Kabir counts his money: ₹50, ₹20, ₹20, ₹10 and ₹5. How much is it in all?
quiz.explain: Start with ₹50, then count on: 70, 90, 100, 105.
quiz.mistake: Counts only one of the ₹20 notes

steps: Add the notes in each choice.
quiz.mistake: Counts the notes instead of adding their values

quiz.q: Meena has two ₹10 coins and three ₹2 coins. How much money does she have?
quiz.explain: Two ₹10 coins = ₹20. Three ₹2 coins = ₹6. ₹20 + ₹6 = ₹26.
quiz.mistake: Counts the number of coins instead of their value

teach.ask: Gappu has one ₹10 note and five ₹1 coins. He says he has ₹6 because there are 6 pieces. Is he right?

teach.nudge: Is a ₹10 note worth the same as a ₹1 coin?

revise.summary: Indian money is counted in rupees (₹). We have coins and notes of different values. Count money starting with the biggest.
focus: Know Indian coins and notes.
Count money by starting with the biggest.
Make an amount in different ways.
traps: Count the value of the coins, not how many coins.
Don't count only one of two equal notes.
Two ₹50 notes make ₹100, not ₹200.

topics.title: Notes: ₹500 and what is on them

learn.hook: Look closely at a ₹100 note. What pictures and words can you spot?
points: Five ₹100 notes make ₹500. Two ₹200 notes and one ₹100 note also make ₹500.
Indian notes show Mahatma Gandhi's picture.
The value is written in numbers and in words.
Notes have special marks, like a shiny thread and raised marks that help people who cannot see well.
Each note of a value has its own colour and size, so it is easy to tell them apart.

example.q: How many ₹100 notes make ₹500?

learn.reallife: Shopkeepers check notes for the thread and marks to make sure they are real.

games.title: Note features
items: Indian notes have Mahatma Gandhi's picture.
His picture is on the front.
The value is written only in numbers.
It is in numbers and in words.
All notes are the same colour.
Each value has its own colour.
Some notes have raised marks to help people who cannot see well.

quiz.q: How many ₹100 notes make ₹500?
Riya has 3 ₹100 notes. How many more ₹100 notes make ₹500?
Which makes ₹500?
steps: Answer: Two ₹200 notes and one ₹100 note

quiz.q: Whose picture is on Indian notes?
quiz.explain: Mahatma Gandhi's picture is on our notes.
steps: Indian notes show the picture of Mahatma Gandhi.

quiz.q: How is the value shown on a note?
quiz.explain: Both numbers and words are printed.
steps: A note shows its value in two ways.

quiz.q: Why do some notes have raised marks?

quiz.explain: People can feel the marks to know the value.

revise.summary: Five ₹100 notes make ₹500. Indian notes show Mahatma Gandhi, the value in numbers and words, and special marks.

Know what is printed on notes.
Know why notes have raised marks.
remember: Value is written in numbers and in words.
Raised marks help people who cannot see well.
traps: Don't leave out a note when adding.
Colour is not the only way the value is shown.
Raised marks are not just decoration.

learn.hook: Welcome to the mela! Kites, balloons and chaat. How much will it all cost?
points: To find the total cost, add the prices.
A bill lists each thing and its price, with the total at the bottom.
Add rupees just like numbers: ₹35 + ₹40 = ₹75.
To buy many of the same thing, add the price again and again: 3 pens at ₹5 each = ₹15.

example.q: At the market, Harpreet buys a kite for ₹25 and a spool of thread for ₹40. What is the total cost?

learn.reallife: When your family shops for groceries, the shopkeeper adds up all the prices on a bill.

quiz.q: A notebook costs ₹30 and a pen costs ₹15. What is the total cost?
quiz.explain: Add the prices: ₹30 + ₹15 = ₹45.

quiz.q: Aisha buys 4 bananas at ₹5 each. How much does she pay?
quiz.explain: 4 bananas at ₹5 each: 5, 10, 15, 20.

quiz.mistake: Adds only two of the three prices

quiz.mistake: Adds 2 to the price instead of doubling it

revise.summary: To find the total cost, add the prices. To buy many of the same thing, add the price again and again.

Check if there is enough money.

Compare whole amounts, not just ones digits.

learn.hook: You pay with a ₹50 note for a ₹35 toy. What does the shopkeeper give back? Your change!
points: When we pay more than the price, the shopkeeper gives back the extra money. This is called change.
Change = money given − price.
₹50 given for a ₹35 toy: the change is ₹50 − ₹35 = ₹15.
Check by counting up from the price: ₹35 + ₹5 = ₹40, and ₹40 + ₹10 = ₹50. So the change is ₹15.

example.q: Arjun gives ₹100 for a book that costs ₹65. How much change should he get?

learn.reallife: Always check your change at a shop. Counting up from the price is a quick way to do it.

games.title: Is the change right?
items: If you pay ₹20 for a ₹20 toy, you get no change.
Change is the price plus the money given.
Change is the money given minus the price.
Paying ₹50 for a ₹42 snack gives ₹8 change.
Paying ₹100 for a ₹55 book gives ₹55 change.
You can check change by adding it to the price.
Price + change should equal the money you gave.

quiz.q: Harpreet pays ₹50 for a toy that costs ₹35. How much change does she get?
quiz.explain: Change = ₹50 − ₹35 = ₹15. Count up: 35 to 40 is 5, 40 to 50 is 10.
quiz.mistake: Adds the price and the money given

quiz.explain: First find the total: ₹40 + ₹30 = ₹70. Then change = ₹100 − ₹70 = ₹30.
quiz.mistake: Gives the total cost instead of the change

quiz.q: Meena paid ₹50 and got ₹15 change. How much did her things cost?
quiz.explain: Price = money given − change = ₹50 − ₹15 = ₹35. Check: ₹35 + ₹15 = ₹50.
quiz.mistake: Adds the change to the money given

quiz.q: Arjun has a ₹200 note. He buys shoes for ₹150. How much change does he get?
quiz.mistake: Adds the price and the money given

quiz.q: Which is the right way to find change?
quiz.explain: Change is the extra money you gave, so take the price away from the money given.
steps: Change is the extra money you gave.
So take the price away from the money given.

teach.ask: Gappu paid ₹20 for a ₹14 seed packet. The shopkeeper gave him some money back. Why, and how much?

teach.nudge: I paid more than the price. How do I find the extra money?

revise.summary: Change is the extra money given back. Change = money given − price. Check by counting up from the price.

learn.hook: Ravi saves ₹45, ₹60 and ₹75 in three weeks. Can he buy a ₹200 cricket bat?

learn.hook: Is 389 + 214 about 400 or about 600? Round to the nearest hundred and see!
points: To estimate, round each number to the nearest hundred.
389 is close to 400. 214 is close to 200. So 389 + 214 is about 400 + 200 = 600.
If the tens digit is 5 or more, round up; if less than 5, round down: 650 → 700, 640 → 600.
For differences: 712 − 289 is about 700 − 300 = 400.
Explain your strategy: 'I rounded both numbers and then added.'

example.q: Estimate 487 + 312.

learn.reallife: Before shopping, families estimate the total bill so they carry enough money.

quiz.q: What is 389 to the nearest hundred?
quiz.explain: 389 is closer to 400 than to 300.
steps: The tens digit is 8, which is 5 or more, so round up.

quiz.q: Estimate 389 + 214.
Estimate 712 − 289.
What is 650 to the nearest hundred?
quiz.explain: When the tens digit is 5, we round up.
steps: The tens digit is 5. When it is 5 or more, round up.

quiz.q: Which is the best estimate for 198 + 403?

quiz.explain: About 300 + 400 = 700. Exactly, it is 707, less than 800.

quiz.q: Estimate 905 − 499.

quiz.explain: Both have 456. 120 is more than 102.

quiz.q: Without subtracting, which is greater?
quiz.explain: Taking away less leaves more.

quiz.q: Which pair has equal value?
quiz.explain: Both are 350.
steps: Both are 350, so they are equal.

quiz.explain: Order does not change a sum, so the missing number is 250.
steps: Changing the order does not change a sum.

quiz.explain: 1 moved from 51 to 199: 200 + 50.

quiz.explain: Taking away 250 leaves less than taking away 205.
steps: Taking away more leaves less, so 700 − 250 is smaller.

learn.hook: Six cards: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Make two 3-digit numbers with the biggest sum!
points: Use digit cards to make two 3-digit numbers, then add or subtract them.
For the biggest sum, put the biggest digits in the hundreds places, then the next in tens, then ones.
With 0-5: hundreds 5 and 4, tens 3 and 2, ones 1 and 0. 531 + 420 = 951.
For the smallest difference, make the hundreds digits next to each other, and keep the rest close. With 0-5: 301 − 254 = 47.

quiz.explain: Biggest digits in the hundreds: 5 and 4. Then 3 and 2. 951.

quiz.q: What is 531 + 420?
What is 301 − 254?
quiz.mistake: Subtracts digit by digit without regrouping

quiz.q: What is 825 + 175?
What is 600 − 82?
For the biggest sum, where should the biggest digits go?
quiz.explain: Hundreds are worth the most.
steps: The hundreds place is worth the most.
So the biggest digits go in the hundreds places.

quiz.q: Cards 2, 5, 8, 1, 4, 7. Make the biggest 3-digit number from three of them.

teach.ask: Gappu has cards 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. How should he place them for the biggest sum of two 3-digit numbers?

Pick the biggest digits for the biggest number.

learn.hook: School closes after the 10th for 12 days of holidays. On which date does it reopen?
points: A month calendar has 7 columns, one for each day of the week, and the dates in rows.
To make a calendar, write 1 under the first day of the month and keep counting along the rows.
To list all the dates of one weekday, go down its column: they are 7 apart, like 3, 10, 17, 24, 31.
Count the Sundays by counting the dates in the Sunday column.
Reopening date: if school closes after the 10th for 12 days, the holidays are the 11th to the 22nd, so it reopens on the 23rd.

example.q: A month has 30 days and the 1st is a Monday. How many Sundays are there?
steps: The next would be 35, which is too far.

learn.reallife: Families mark festivals, birthdays and exam dates on a wall calendar.

games.title: Calendar facts
items: Dates in one column of a calendar are 7 apart.

Every month starts on a Sunday.
If the 2nd is a Friday, the 9th is a Friday.

quiz.q: The 1st of a month is a Monday. Which date is the first Sunday?

steps: Mon 1, Tue 2, Wed 3, Thu 4, Fri 5, Sat 6, Sun 7.

quiz.explain: 29 is a Monday, 30 a Tuesday, 31 a Wednesday.

revise.summary: A month calendar has 7 columns, one for each day. Dates in one column are 7 apart, so we can find all the dates of a weekday.
focus: Make a month calendar.
Find all dates of one weekday.
Count holidays and find a reopening date.
remember: Closed after the 10th for 12 days: reopens on the 23rd.
traps: Not every month has 4 of each day. Some have 5.

learn.hook: When is your birthday? When is Diwali? A calendar helps us know!
points: A week has 7 days: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday and Sunday.
A year has 12 months, from January to December.
April, June, September and November have 30 days. February has 28 days, or 29 in a leap year. All the other months have 31 days.
A calendar shows the date of each day in a month.
The same day comes again every 7 days. If the 3rd is a Monday, the 10th is a Monday too.

example.q: The 12th of a month is a Thursday. What day is the 19th of that month?

learn.reallife: We use calendars to plan holidays, festivals, birthdays and exams.

quiz.q: How many days are there in a week?
quiz.explain: Monday to Sunday makes 7 days.
steps: Days: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday.

quiz.q: How many months are there in a year?
quiz.explain: January to December makes 12 months.
steps: Months go from January to December.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up months in a year with days in a week

quiz.q: Which month comes right after June?
quiz.explain: The months go ... May, June, July, August ... So July comes after June.
steps: The months go ... May, June, July, August ...
quiz.mistake: Picks the month before instead of after

quiz.q: How many days does April have?
quiz.explain: April is one of the four months with 30 days: April, June, September and November.
steps: April, June, September and November have 30 days.

quiz.q: Today is Friday. What day will it be tomorrow?
quiz.explain: After Friday comes Saturday.
steps: Days in order: ... Thursday, Friday, Saturday ...

quiz.q: If the 5th of a month is a Tuesday, what day is the 12th of the same month?
quiz.explain: 12 − 5 = 7 days, which is 1 week. So the 12th is also a Tuesday.
quiz.mistake: Counts on 7 days but lands one day off

quiz.q: Which month has only 28 days in most years?
quiz.explain: February is the shortest month. It has 28 days, and 29 in a leap year.
steps: It has 28 days, and 29 in a leap year.
quiz.mistake: Does not know that February is the short month

quiz.q: Kabir's holiday is 2 weeks long. How many days is that?
quiz.explain: 1 week is 7 days, so 2 weeks is 7 + 7 = 14 days.

teach.ask: Gappu wants to know how long a week and a year are. Can you explain the calendar to him?

revise.summary: A week has 7 days and a year has 12 months. Months have 30 or 31 days, and February has 28 (29 in a leap year).
focus: Know the days and months in order.

remember: February: 28, or 29 in a leap year. Others: 31.

2 weeks is 14 days, not 9.

learn.hook: Your birthday was on a Monday last year. Will it be on Monday this year too?
points: Some things stay the same every year: the names of the 12 months, their order, and 7 days in a week.
Some things change: the day of the week for a date, and the dates of many festivals like Diwali or Holi.
A year has 365 days. A leap year has 366 days (February has 29 days).
A year has about 52 weeks: 52 weeks is 364 days, and 1 or 2 days are left over.
Because of those extra days, a date usually moves one day of the week ahead next year.

example.q: A year has 365 days. How many full weeks and extra days?

learn.reallife: Diwali comes on a different date every year, but Independence Day is always on 15 August.

quiz.q: About how many weeks are in a year?
steps: So a year has about 52 weeks.

quiz.q: Which stays the same every year?

Know days in a year and in a leap year.
Find how a date's weekday moves next year.
remember: 52 weeks = 364 days, so 1 day is left over.
A date usually moves one weekday ahead next year.
traps: Don't forget the extra day: 365, not 364.
Holi and Diwali dates change.
A birthday does not stay on the same weekday.

learn.hook: Didi is twice as old as Raju and 10 years older. How old are they?
points: To find age from a date of birth: subtract the birth year from the current year (after the birthday has passed).
Born in 2018, in 2026 after the birthday: 2026 − 2018 = 8 years old.
Puzzle: 'twice as old and 10 years older' means the younger one's age is the 10 years. So 10 and 20.
Every year, everyone gets 1 year older. The difference between two ages never changes.

example.q: Amma was 25 when Mira was born. Mira is 8 now. How old is Amma?

learn.reallife: Birthdays are celebrated with cake and the number of candles tells the age!

items.q: Twice as old and 10 years older: younger?
Twice as old and 6 years older: older?

games.title: Age facts
items: The age gap between two people stays the same every year.
If I am 8 now, I will be 10 in 2 years.
If Didi is twice my age now, she will always be twice my age.
Twice changes, but the gap stays.
Born in 2017, I am 9 in 2026 after my birthday.

quiz.q: Arjun was born in 2018. How old is he in 2026, after his birthday?

Didi is 10 years older, so Raju is 10.

quiz.q: Same puzzle: how old is Didi?
steps: Raju is 10 (the younger one's age is the 10 years).

quiz.q: Mother is twice as old as her son and 30 years older. How old is the son?
quiz.explain: If the son is 30, the mother is 60. 60 is twice 30 and 30 more.

So the son's age is the 30 years.

revise.summary: To find age, subtract the birth year from the current year after the birthday. Everyone gets 1 year older each year, so age gaps never change.

Don't halve the gap in 'twice as old' puzzles.

learn.hook: A birth certificate says 14/11/2018. What does that tell you?
points: Dates are often written day/month/year: 14/11/2018 means 14 November 2018.
The middle number is the month: 01 is January, 11 is November, 12 is December.
From the date of birth, find the age in a year, and the date of the birthday every year (14 November).
Count months between two dates: 5 March to 5 July is 4 months. Count days: 3 June to 20 June is 17 days.
Make your own record: your date of birth, first day of school, and other important dates.

quiz.q: How many days from 3 June to 20 June?

teach.praise: Day 9, month 3: my birthday is 9 March! Chirp!
teach.nudge: Which number is the day and which is the month?

revise.summary: Dates are written day/month/year. From a birth certificate we find the birthday and the age in a given year.

Find age from a date of birth.
Count months and days between dates.
remember: 5 March to 5 July = 4 months. 3 June to 20 June = 17 days.
traps: Don't read the day as the month.
Don't put the month first.
Don't count March when counting months from 5 March.

learn.hook: Tick, tock! The clock tells us when to wake up, eat lunch and play cricket. Let's learn to read it!
points: A clock has a short hand that shows the hour and a long hand that shows the minutes.
When the long hand points to 12, it is an o'clock time. Short hand on 3 means 3 o'clock.
When the long hand points to 6, it is half past. Half past 4 is 30 minutes after 4 o'clock.
1 hour = 60 minutes. Half an hour = 30 minutes.
The long hand goes all the way round once in 1 hour.

example.q: The long hand is on 6 and the short hand is between 4 and 5. What time is it?
steps: The long hand on 6 means half past.
The short hand has gone past 4 but not reached 5.

learn.reallife: School starts, trains leave and TV shows begin at fixed times on the clock.

revise.summary: A clock has a short hand for hours and a long hand for minutes. Long hand on 12 means o'clock; on 6 means half past.
focus: Read o'clock and half past times.
Know which hand shows what.
Find how long something takes in hours.
remember: 1 hour = 60 minutes. Half an hour = 30 minutes.
Long hand on 12: o'clock. On 6: half past.
The long hand goes round once in 1 hour.
traps: Don't read the long hand as the hour.
Half an hour is 30 minutes, not 50.
At half past 11, the short hand is between 11 and 12; it is not half past 12.

learn.hook: Cut a clock face like a pizza into 4 equal slices. Each slice is a quarter of an hour!
points: A clock face can be split into 4 quarters. Each quarter is 15 minutes.
Quarter past 2: the long hand is on 3. It is 15 minutes after 2 o'clock.
Quarter to 5: the long hand is on 9. It is 15 minutes before 5 o'clock.
Each number on the clock is 5 minutes for the long hand: on 1 it is 5 minutes, on 2 it is 10 minutes.
We can also write times like 2:15, 2:30 and 4:45.

example.q: The long hand is on 9 and the short hand is close to 8. What time is it?
steps: The long hand on 9 means quarter to.
The short hand is nearly at 8, so 8 o'clock is coming.
15 minutes before 8 o'clock is quarter to 8, or 7:45.

learn.reallife: Your mother may say 'Be ready by quarter to 9!' Now you will know exactly when that is.
